paragraphs.source_en: The ‘empire’s longest century’ was marked by the creation of a new class of bureaucrats who aimed to guide the empire through Reform 345 a period of administrative and legal reorganisation and reform.

units.source_en: The ‘empire’s longest century’ was marked by the creation of a new class of bureaucrats who aimed to guide the empire through Reform 345 a period of administrative and legal reorganisation and reform.

paragraphs.source_en: The objective was to centralise the bureaucratic system and increase control through newly developed technologies and agency specialisation, including the establishment of new provincial and urban administrative bureaus. This led to widened public control of administration, diffusion of authority, and the entrance of new people into the realm of administration. The many edicts and laws issued by the sultan during this period introduced new state primary and secondary schools, open to all irrespective of religion. Prior to this, each religious community had been responsible for educating its children in its own religion and language. Law was also secularised. Formerly, Islamic law courts, which applied Islamic and secular law, had been supreme, but now secular courts were introduced, and as their jurists grew in prominence, Islamic jurists began to lose their power.

The economy was liberalised, the right to private property protected.

paragraphs.source_en: The changes even affected the timeworn practice of slavery. Abdiilmecid I closed the Istanbul slave market and ended the trade in African slaves, but without ever completely abolishing slavery. Circassian girls continued to stock the private homes of the Ottoman elite.

paragraphs.source_en: In 1839, Abdiilmecid I promulgated the Decree of the Rose Garden. The decree guaranteed ‘security for life, honour, and property’ of all subjects, and a ‘regular system of assessing taxes’.*° Tax collection would no longer be based on tax farming, through which a tax farmer could abuse his grant to obtain taxes by demanding amounts greater than what he was required to submit 346 THE OTTOMANS to the central treasury. That practice was criticised in the words of the decree as ‘handing over-the financial and political affairs of a country to the whims of an ordinary man and perhaps to the grasp of force and oppression, for if the tax farmer is not of good character he will be interested only in his own profit and will behave oppressively’.
